def: Deciding who gets a treatment by a chance mechanism (a coin flip or a hash of the user ID), so the groups are balanced on average on every trait, measured or not.
A difference between treated and comparison groups that exists before treatment, so the naive comparison mixes the effect with who ended up in each group. Opt-in betas are the classic case.
Units choose their own treatment, so whatever drives the choice (engagement, motivation) also differs between the groups.

Units picked for an extreme measurement tend to be less extreme next time, because part of the extreme was luck. Expected bounce is (1 − ρ) times the distance from the mean, with ρ the test–retest correlation.
Analysing every unit in the arm it was assigned to, whether or not it used the treatment. It keeps the protection randomization gives; filtering after assignment does not.
The framework that gives each unit an outcome under treatment, Y(1), and under control, Y(0); the causal effect is their difference, of which only one is ever observed.
A study that estimates a causal effect without random assignment by exploiting a situation that mimics it (a cutoff, a lottery, a staggered launch), at the price of an untestable assumption.
Estimates an effect as the treated group's change minus the comparison group's change over the same period, which removes stable differences between groups and shared trends.
The assumption behind difference-in-differences: without treatment, the treated and comparison groups would have changed by the same amount. Checked, partially, by plotting the pre-period.
Compares units just above and just below a cutoff that decides treatment; valid if units cannot precisely control which side they land on. The estimate applies near the cutoff.
The probability of receiving treatment given observed covariates, e(x) = P(T=1 | X=x). Matching or weighting on it balances measured covariates only.
Pairing each treated unit with similar untreated units on pre-treatment covariates; assumes no unmeasured confounders and enough overlap.

A variable that shifts treatment, is as good as random, and affects the outcome only through treatment. The Wald estimator divides its effect on the outcome by its effect on treatment, giving the effect for compliers.

Fits the pre-launch trend and seasonality of a metric and reads the effect as the post-launch gap from that forecast. Anything else that changed on the same date is indistinguishable from the treatment.
Builds a weighted blend of untreated units that tracks the treated unit before treatment and uses it as the counterfactual afterwards (Abadie, Diamond and Hainmueller, 2010).

Grouping similar units (by tier, language, prompt) and randomizing within each group, which removes chance imbalance on the blocking variable and cuts variance by about the share it explains. Also called stratified randomization.
The thing the coin flip decides about: request, session, user, or cluster. The variance calculation must account for it, or error bars come out too narrow.
Randomizing whole groups (orgs, regions, workspaces) instead of individuals, usually to contain spillover; power depends on the number of clusters.
Stable unit treatment value assumption: each unit's outcome depends only on its own treatment (no interference) and each treatment comes in one version.
When one unit's treatment changes another unit's outcome, such as through shared GPU capacity, shared documents, or a marketplace. Also called spillover; it violates SUTVA.
An experiment that flips the whole system between treatment and control in time blocks, used when units share capacity or a market; blocks must outlast carryover.
Arm sizes that differ from the planned split by more than chance, detected with a chi-square test; it signals broken assignment or logging, and results should not be read until it is explained.
The difference in a covariate's mean between arms divided by the pooled standard deviation; a common balance check flags |SMD| above 0.1.
Numbers or words used only as names (club, model family, error category). Counts, proportions, and the mode are meaningful; averages are not.
Values with a meaningful order but unequal or unknown gaps (finishing place, 1–5 rating). Medians, percentiles, and rank tests are meaningful.
Equal steps with an arbitrary zero (Celsius, Elo-style ratings). Differences and means are meaningful; ratios are not.
Equal steps and a true zero (time, tokens, cost), so ratios, logs, and geometric means are meaningful.
Stevens's (1946) classification of scales as nominal, ordinal, interval, or ratio, defined by which transformations leave the information unchanged.
A rating scale with ordered response options such as 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree). Whether single items may be averaged is a long-running debate.
A rank-based test of whether values from one group tend to exceed values from another; its effect size is P(B > A) + ½P(tie). It compares medians only if the two shapes match.
The paired counterpart of Mann–Whitney: ranks the absolute per-item differences and compares the sums for positive and negative differences.
A model (cumulative logit or probit) that treats an ordinal outcome as a latent continuous score cut by thresholds; handles covariates and clustering without assuming equal gaps.
Knowing only that a value exceeds some limit, such as a run that hit the time cap or a user still active when data ends. Dropping or capping censored values biases summaries downward.
Estimates the survival curve from censored durations as the product, over event times, of the share of at-risk units that survive each event (Kaplan and Meier, 1958).
Compares two or more survival curves using all event times; loses power when the curves cross.
Approximates the variance of a function of estimates, such as a ratio of means, from their variances and covariance; the standard way to get error bars on ratio metrics randomized by user.
A metric that divides two totals, such as successes per request, where the randomization unit (user) differs from the analysis unit (request).
How consistently a measurement gives the same result when repeated: test–retest correlation, inter-rater agreement, or ICC. Necessary for validity, not sufficient.
Whether a measurement captures what it claims to: content (covers the domain), criterion (predicts a trusted outcome), and construct (measures the concept in its name).
The correlation between repeated measurements of the same items under the same conditions, such as an eval run twice with different seeds or judge samples.
How often independent raters agree on the same items, usually reported as raw agreement plus a chance-corrected statistic such as Cohen's kappa or Krippendorff's alpha.
Noise in a predictor biases its estimated slope toward zero by the reliability factor λ, and noise in two variables shrinks their correlation by √(λ<sub>X</sub>λ<sub>Y</sub>) (Spearman, 1904).
The gap between a recorded value and the true one. Classical error inflates variance and attenuates slopes; error correlated with treatment or outcome causes bias.
An easy-to-measure stand-in for a target that is slow, costly, or rare (thumbs-up for satisfaction, judge score for expert judgment). Optimizing it can drive it apart from the target.
Medicine's term for a proxy outcome. A surrogate correlated with the target can still mislead if the treatment moves it through a path that does not reach the target.
